Beneath the Blue Paint

[A] I was waiting for my sister in the workshop of the Bellweather Theater when I noticed a long wooden sign resting across two padded tables. Its blue surface was split near one corner, and several letters had faded almost completely. I assumed it was waiting to be discarded away[1]. The theater's conservator, Ms. Okafor, corrected me: the sign had hung above the building's entrance for most of a century.

[B] She directed a lamp across the surface and invited me closer. Under the blue paint, thin shapes appeared like sleepy lines barely waking beneath ice[2]. Ms. Okafor explained that the sign had been repainted whenever the building changed owners. The theater companies chose new names and covered the old ones, but traces of its[3] lettering remained in the shallow grain.

Using a cotton swab dampened with solvent, she tested a square no larger than a postage stamp. The first exposed letter ended in a curling stroke unlike the theater's current block lettering.[4] Leaning over the table, the gold edge was revealed by Ms. Okafor one millimeter at a time.[5] A second curved line emerged beneath it. Together, the marks formed part of the word Lyric, the name of a music hall that had occupied the building decades before the present theater.

[C] I asked why she did not simply uncover the oldest layer and remove everything above it. Ms. Okafor shook her head, each coat[6] belonged to the sign's history. Choosing one era would erase evidence of the others. Instead, she planned to reveal narrow windows into several layers while stabilizing the cracked wood. She describes[7] the finished sign as a timeline that could be read without flattening its past into one date.

At first, the overlapping names had looked like damage to me. Gradually, however, the exposed fragments began to resemble a conversation among the building's former lives.[8] [D] A photograph in the theater archive showed the Lyric sign glowing above a crowd in 1948.[9] When my sister arrived, I stepped around the table once more before leaving. I no longer saw a ruined blue board; I saw a surface whose worn places had learned to hold more than one story.[10]
